Article Title: AITA presidential election: Chintan Parekh vs Rohit Rajpal - two visions for Indian tennis
Article Text:

2. Infrastructure development

3. More tournaments at domestic and international level

BOTTOM LINE: Two visions, one challenge

NEW DELHI: The race for the All India Tennis Association (AITA) presidency pits Chintan Parekh's "Tennis First" motto against Rohit Rajpal's "The Next Serve," with both candidates promising to address Indian tennis' structural challenges.While Parekh's pitch centres on governance reform, financial sustainability and expanding tennis beyond established centres; Rajpal has outlined a more programme-driven roadmap with specific proposals, timelines and targets. Their approaches differ on how to tackle key issues confronting Indian tennis.Chintan Parekh wants to expand talent scouting beyond established centres, with a focus on underserved regions such as the North-East. His vision includes coaching pyramids and grooming young players for a stronger tennis ecosystem by 2030.Rohit Rajpal proposes a state-wise development audit within 100 days, common talent-identification protocols, zonal camps, a central player database and low-cost talent scouting in underserved districts.Chintan Parekh wants to take tennis to regions lacking infrastructure, particularly beyond metropolitan centres, and tap talent in remote and underserved areas.Rohit Rajpal plans to expand national and zonal centres of excellence, partner state associations, develop infrastructure in the Northeast and hill regions, and explore a high-altitude training centre.Chintan Parekh focuses on strengthening AITA's finances to fund tennis development, but has not outlined specific targets for tournament expansion.Rohit Rajpal wants to bring ATP and WTA events back to India, expand Challenger, ITF and junior tournaments, rotate events across zones, and build women's and senior circuits with at least 30 tournaments annually by 2030.Chintan Parekh identifies better governance as the key pillar under his presidency. He promises transparent, player-centric governance and a clean-up of AITA's institutional structure. He wants the AITA Trust to be brought under the association's umbrella, its trustees restructured, and issues concerning AITA's relationship with Delhi Lawn Tennis Association (DLTA) resolved.Rohit Rajpal proposes published accounts, budgets and fund utilisation, along with Athletes, Ethics and Dispute Resolution committees. He also promises transparent selection criteria, calendars and measurable progress reports.Chintan Parekh wants to build AITA's corpus to ₹200-250 crore over four years, tap CSR funding and create greater financial capacity to support budding players."Our vision is a very clean AITA with a focus on the players. Grassroots development is important so scholarships for talented children in rural areas(is one target).Tennis is still considered an affluent sport, one for the elite. The first step is to clean it up (the corruption). The second step is to build the grassroots, then get the funding in, empower the state associations who empower the players," Leander Paes , who is the vice-presidential candidate in Parekh's team, had told select media after filing his nomination.Rohit Rajpal proposes travel and tournament-entry assistance for professionals, a CSR-funded Players' Distress Fund and a feasibility study for a pension scheme for retired players.Parekh's pitch is centred on institutional reform, financial strength and widening tennis' reach. Rajpal's manifesto offers a structured roadmap with programmes, timelines and measurable targets.Both promise to address Indian tennis' longstanding challenges. The real test, however, will be turning those promises into tangible opportunities for players.
Article Summary: Parekh's pitch is centred on institutional reform, financial strength and widening tennis' reach. Rajpal's manifesto offers a roadmap with programmes and measurable targets. Both promise to address Indian tennis' longstanding challenges. The test will be turning those promises into real opportunities for players.

Article Title: ILT20: Dubai Capitals beat Desert Vipers by 45 runs, register first win of season 5
Article Text:
Noor Ahmad of Dubai Capitals celebrates the wicket of Shimron Hetmyer of Desert Vipers during the Match 6 of the International League T20 Season 5 between Dubai Capitals and Desert Vipers. (Photo/ILT20)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Dubai Capitals defeated Desert Vipers by 45 runs at the Dubai International Stadium on Wednesday to register their first win of ILT20 season 5. Sam Billings ' 43 off 31 balls and Rovman Powell 's rapid 28 off 12 powered the Capitals to 164/7, before the bowlers took over. Noor Ahmad 's four for 20 and Mustafizur Rahman 's two for 12 led the way, with Dushmantha Chameera (2/27) and Hassan Khan (2/16) also taking two wickets each as the Vipers were bowled out for 119 in 17.5 overs. Andries Gous's 27 off 30 was the Vipers' top score.Put in to bat first, Dubai Capitals suffered an early blow when Masood Gurbaz (2 off 2) was run out after a mix-up with Faf du Plessis (24 off 30) to leave them at 8/1. Max Holden (22 off 17) joined du Plessis and steered the innings through the powerplay, with a stand of 37 runs in 34 balls.The partnership didn't last as Vipers skipper Shadab Khan had Max Holden caught in the seventh. Soon after, du Plessis, was stumped off Nangeyalia Khan in search of his first boundary of the innings.The Capitals were 61/3 in 9.4 overs when Sam Billings (43 off 31) and Marcus Stoinis (27 off 24) came together for a key stand of 59 runs in 40 balls. With boundaries hard to come by, Billings broke the shackles in the 16th to smash Shadab for a six and two fours.Just as the Capitals looked set for a big finish, Khuzaima Tanveer removed Stoinis to leave the score at 120/4 in 16.2 overs.He then scalped Billings and Karim Janat (6 off 4) in the 19th over to emerge as the pick of the Vipers attack and take over the White Belt (awarded to the best bowler) with eight wickets in three innings.Rovman Powell (28 off 12) provided the finishing touch with a rapid-fire knock, smashing two fours and two sixes including 16 in the final over to catapult the Capitals to 164/7 in 20 overs.In response, the Vipers lost Babar Azam (1 off 2) in the second over off Dushmantha Chameera's bowling to leave them at 2/1. Fakhar Zaman (12 off 11) and Andries Gous added 35 before Fakhar was caught off Mustafizur Rahman in the fifth over, making it 37/2.Noor Ahmad then took charge, removing Joe Clarke (3 off 5) in the seventh and Gous (27 off 30) in the ninth over to leave the Vipers on 48/4.Shimron Hetmyer (19 off 13) and Shadab (16 off 11) tried to rebuild with a 31-run stand, but Chameera ended it by having the Vipers skipper caught in the 12th over. Noor had Hetmyer stumped in the 13th, leaving the Vipers at 83/6.Tom Curran (18 off 8) briefly raised hopes with two fours and a six, but he was caught off Noor for his fourth wicket in the 15th over to make it 102/7.Hassan Khan then struck twice in the 17th with the wickets of Khuzaima Tanveer (9 off 7) and Nangeyalia Khan (6 off 12). Mustafizur returned to dismiss Mujeeb Ur Rahman (2 off 4) as the Vipers were bowled out for 119 in 17.5 overs.
Article Summary: Dubai Capitals defeated Desert Vipers by 45 runs at the Dubai International Stadium on Wednesday to register their first win of ILT20 season 5. Sam Billings'43 off 31 balls and Rovman Powell's rapid 28 off 12 powered the Capitals to 164/7, before the bowlers took over. Noor Ahmad's four for 20 and Mustafizur Rahman's two for 12 led the way, with Dushmantha Chameera and Hassan Khan also taking two wickets each as the Vipers were bowled out for 119 in 17.5 overs.

Article Title: World Chess Championship: Gukesh draws second game against Javokhir Sindarov in 20 moves; score tied 1-1
Article Text:
Indian defending champion D Gukesh competes against Uzbekistan's challenger Javokhir Sindarov during the first game of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026, in Geneva, Switzerland. (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

D Gukesh settled for a draw with white against Uzbekistan's Javokhir Sindarov in the second game of the FIDE World Championship in Geneva on Wednesday, with the contest ending after just 20 moves.The reigning world champion, who is not usually known for agreeing to early draws, opted for a repetition of moves after spending some time in the middle game. The two players shared the point, taking their tally to one each after two games of the 14-game match.Playing with white for the first time in the match, Gukesh opened with the London System, possibly looking for a more cautious approach after facing pressure in the opening game, where Sindarov had pushed for an advantage but could not convert it.However, Sindarov was able to equalise through a series of straightforward moves, leaving little room for either player to gain an edge in the middle game. The two exchanged a pair of minor pieces, but all 30 remaining pieces were still on the board when they agreed to a draw.Gukesh's 14th move drew attention, allowing Sindarov to advance a kingside pawn on his next turn by pushing his bishop's pawn forward. Some commentators felt the move had unsettled the Indian.Gukesh responded with a move to stop the pawn's progress, but Sindarov was not under any real pressure thereafter.The players repeated their moves soon after, bringing the game to a close. Sindarov arguably had the better of the opening exchanges, with Gukesh's London System failing to give him any meaningful advantage.With 12 games still to be played in the 14-game match, Sindarov will have the white pieces in the third game and will look to press for an advantage.Asked after the game about his choice of the London System and the quick draw, Gukesh said: "Well it’s a good opening and nowadays everything from both colours are so much playable...so much to explore because of the engines. So, I don’t think one opening is better than the other...it would be a nice way to start the match (with London System)."Asked whether he was frustrated by Sindarov's solid play and the lack of opportunities to push for a win, Gukesh said both players were so well prepared for the championship that a "formal outcome" was to be expected."Yeah, I felt I could have remembered more from my notes, but okay it's like both players are super well prepared and getting nothing out of the opening is a very formal outcome in a wold championship," said Gukesh.He added that he had hoped to catch Sindarov off guard with the London System, but the Uzbek was well prepared and proved a tough opponent."London, I thought, would be a little surprise early in the match, but well done to my opponent, he was prepared and he was tough. London as an opening, I mean somewhere I was playing it quite a bit maybe in the lockdown pandemic so...some nostalgic opening," he said, explaining his choice of the London System.The first player to reach 7.5 points will be crowned champion. In case of a tie after 14 games, shorter-format tiebreak games will be played to determine the winner.The time control is 120 minutes for the first 40 moves, with an additional 30 minutes and a 30-second increment per move from move 41. Draws by mutual agreement are not permitted before the completion of 40 moves. However, a game can end earlier through threefold repetition or stalemate.The total prize fund for the match is USD 2.5 million. Each win is worth USD 200,000, with the remaining prize money to be shared equally. If the match goes into tiebreaks, the winner will take home USD 1.3 million, while the runner-up will receive USD 1.2 million.
Article Summary: Defending champion D Gukesh settled for a draw with Uzbekistan's Javokhir Sindarov in the second game of the FIDE World Championship in Geneva. The two players shared the point, taking their tally to one each after two games of the 14-game match.

Article Title: 'Nostalgic opening from lockdown days': Gukesh explains London System choice
Article Text:

D Gukesh, with white, was not really happy about a soft draw one that allowed Javokhir Sindarov equality and almost forced another draw with repetition of moves.The second game of the 14-game World Chess Championship match between the Indian champion and Uzbek challenger ended in a peace treaty inside two hours and just 20 moves of the London System opening (3.Bf4) in Geneva on Wednesday. Except a knight each, the other 30 pieces were on the board (15 each) when the game ended tamely.Before coming out of the players’ lounge to the fan zone and to the press conference, Gukesh was in a mood of self reflection and did not appear happy with how things had panned out despite having the advantage of white pieces. But he regrouped quickly and managed more than a smile while giving a quick reaction to the official broadcast and detailed answers at the media conference.“Away from the board, I have been much happier compared to Singapore (the match against Ding Liren in 2024),” said Gukesh.On how different it is to be at the match without his father accompanying him and instead, with his Bengaluru-based designer friends Shikhar and Charmie, Gukesh said, “Being with friends takes away a lot of the stress. Happy they are here. Also Gayo (second Gajewski) is here and is doing a lot of work.Happy with the setup for this match.”Gukesh opting for the London system is not suspect, but has been played only twice in World Championship matches (Ding beat Nepo in 2022 and Gukesh and Ding split a point in 2024). Though the opening was a mild surprise, Sindarov was up to the task and on the Uzbek’s prepared line (7..Qb6), Gukesh laughed, “I could not recollect what I was doing here. I felt I could have remembered more from my notes ... It was my nostalgic opening from the lockdown days. ”“There is a lot of theory in London (system) too. But it was not some deep strategy (to play this).”Gukesh explained that the position was such that he could always hope that Sindarov could go wrong had they continued to play (and avoid three-fold repetition) but it's likely that even he himself could go wrong and there was not much in the position.Black’s 15th move (f5) invited a long thought from Gukesh and after about 30 minutes he responded with f3 and fell about 35 minutes behind needing to make 24 more moves in about 50 mins. Earlier, a new position on the board was reached after Sindarov's queen retreat (Qd8) on the 11th move.The third game will be played on Thursday before Friday’s rest day with Gukesh having black pieces.Moves (Game 2):D Gukesh vs Javokhir Sindarov -- 1. d4 d5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Bf4 c5 4. e3 e6 5. Nbd2 Nc6 6. c3 Be7 7. Ne5 Qb6 8. Rb1 Nxe5 9. Bxe5 Bd7 10. a4 O-O 11. Bd3 Qd8 12. O-O Rc8 13. Ra1 Be8 14. Qe2 Nd7 15. Bg3 f5 16. f3 Nf6 17. Be5 Nd7 18. Bg3 Nf6 19. Be5 Nd7 20. Bg3 Nf6.Game drawn

The second game of the 14-game World Chess Championship match between the Indian champion and Uzbek challenger ended in a peace treaty inside two hours and just 20 moves of the London System opening (3.Bf4)

Article Title: Treesa Jolly-Gayatri Gopichand duo begins title defence with easy win
Article Text:
Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand

LUCKNOW: Defending champions Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand began their bid for a hat-trick of titles with a comfortable victory as Indian shuttlers made a strong start to the Syed Modi India International Super 300 badminton on Wednesday.The World Championships bronze medallists brushed aside qualifiers Rashmi Ganesh and Amrutha Pramuthesh 21-8, 21-7 in the opening round.Speaking about the playing conditions, Treesa said the pair took some time to adjust in their opening match.“The conditions were slow and slightly tricky. In the second game, our opponents also played some good rallies and challenged us. We stayed patient, played longer rallies and tried to understand the court and atmosphere better since it was our first match,” she said.Gayatri, meanwhile, said the crowd support in Lucknow had given the pair an added boost.“We have received tremendous support from the crowd, and that gives us a lot of confidence.”
Article Summary: Defending champions Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand beat Rashmi Ganesh and Amrutha Pramuthesh 21-8, 21-7 in the opening round of the Syed Modi India International Super 300 badminton tournament.

Article Title: Mrithika’s golden run continues at BIMSTEC meet
Article Text:
Mrithika

KOLKATA: Mrithika T continued her brilliant showing this year as she won the women’s 100m gold on the opening day of the BIMSTEC Under-23 Athletics Meet at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar.Mrithika, hailing from Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu, clocked 12.02s to narrowly edge past Sri Lanka’s K. Risansa Hirupama (12.07s). Bangladesh’s Dewan Sumaya (12.24s) won bronze. Interestingly, the 17-year-old wasn’t initially selected for the individual 100m, so naturally her coach was more than happy after she finished on top of the podium on Wednesday.“I didn’t even know she would be running the 100m here. Until yesterday, I only knew that she had been selected for the 4x100m relay. We hadn’t prepared specifically for the 100m, so I’m very happy that she won the gold medal,” said coach Parthiban.As for Mrithika, who broke the 100m meet record at the National Youth Championships in September (11.78s) and then clocked a lifetime best of 11.71s at the National Junior Championships in Oct, she couldn’t have been more excited.“I want to thank my coach, who has supported me right from the beginning, and my father.He has always supported me and has been my backbone. If he wasn’t there, I wouldn’t be here today,” said the Class XII student of Brindhavan Vidhyalaya Public School in Coimbatore.It was her father, Thirugnanajothi, who inspired Mrithika to take up the sport, and he still makes sure to drop her off for her 5am training sessions. “My mother also gets up very early in the morning to prepare my diet and food. My parents have done so much for me, and I’m very thankful to them,” she added.Besides Mrithika, India won five more gold medals on the opening day.Among the men, Anurag Singh Kaler won the shot put with a throw of 18.34m, Daksh Bishnoi won the triple jump with a leap of 15.58m, while Hitesh clinched the 1500m title.Among the women, Priya (52.03m) and Nikita Kumari (50.02m) led an Indian one-two in the discus throw. In the final race of the day, the women’s 5000m, India’s Sonam Parmar (17:31.12) and Sunita Devi (17:31.66) fought a tight race to win gold and silver, respectively.Sri Lanka’s K. Niduki Prarthana (17:47.07) was third.Sri Lanka, meanwhile, won two gold medals, with Dineth Induwara Weraratna claiming the men’s 100m title in 10.35s. India’s Rushiprasad Desai (10.46s) finished second, while Sri Lanka’s Saad Jamaldeen (10.57s) also made the podium.Nethya Sampath Jonikku won the other gold for the island nation in the high jump with a leap of 2.08m, while India’s Binoy B and Ambriesh K, who also cleared 2.08m, finished second and third, respectively.
Article Summary: Mrithika T won the women's 100m gold on the opening day of the BIMSTEC Under-23 Athletics Meet at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar. The 17-year-old, hailing from Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu, clocked 12.02s to narrowly edge past Sri Lanka’s K. Risansa Hirupama (12.07s)

Article Title: AFC Champions League: Jeakson’s late strike fuels East Bengal’s knockout hopes
Article Text:
Jeakson Singh (second from right) scores East Bengal’s winner against Al-Hussein at Salt Lake Stadium.

KOLKATA: Sometimes, football defies logic. East Bengal FC’s historic 1-0 win against Jordanian champions Al-Hussein SC in the reverse fixture of their AFC Champions League Two clash here on Tuesday — a first by an Indian club since the continent’s second-tier club tournament was rebranded in 2024 — was one such moment.After living on the edge for most of the contest and getting rescued by the woodwork four times, East Bengal somehow flipped the script. They earned a corner in the 87th minute — their first in the second session — and Bashim Rashid whipped in a well-measured delivery towards the first post. David Lalhlansanga deftly placed the ball in front of Jeakson Singh, who fired home.After two draws and two losses, East Bengal kept their hopes of advancing to the round of 16 alive with this win. They will travel to face Group D leaders Al Shorta of Iraq on Dec. 8. Only the top two from each group will make the knockouts.
Article Summary: East Bengal FC beat Jordanian champions Al-Hussein SC 1-0. Jeakson Singh scored the winner in the 87th minute at Salt Lake Stadium. It was the first AFC Champions League Two win by an Indian club since the continent’s second-tier club tournament was rebranded in 2024.

Article Title: ‘ICC, boards need to step in’: Harbhajan Singh on India-Pakistan cricket skirmishes
Article Text:
Harbhajan Singh has joined the chorus of those voicing their concern at the deteriorating player behaviour during India-Pakistan clashes.

'Have some patience with Team India'

MUMBAI: The last couple of India-Pakistan cricket contests, while they've provided plenty of excitement, have also seen ugly scenes of skirmishes between the players. On November 14, India's Under-19 players had a go at their Pakistani counterparts, celebrating wildly and overenthusiastically after pipping their arch-rivals by one wicket in a thrilling Under-19 Asia Cup final at Al Amerat in Oman. On November 22 (Sunday) in Doha, players of both India A and Pakistan A (Pakistani Shaheens) exchanged verbal volleys with each other, with India A pacer Harshit Rana involved in heated altercations with the Pakistan players during their Asia Cup Rising Stars match in Doha, which Pakistan A won by 48 runs.After the ugly scenes witnessed in the Asia Cup Under-19 final, former India skipper Dilip Vengsarkar had told TOI about the need for the BCCI to educate young cricketers at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence about behaving well on the field while playing for India at any level. India's off-spin great Harbhajan Singh has joined the chorus of those voicing their concern at the deteriorating player behaviour during these clashes and has urged the game's authorities — the International Cricket Council and the BCCI — to "step in" to check the trend of players from both countries getting carried away in Indo-Pak cricket matches."Somewhere down the line, the ICC needs to step in. I think it is just getting a bit too much with the reactions. First, Pakistan's boys did it (after beating India Under-19s in the league stage). Then the Indians won and did it. And then yesterday too, whatever happened was not right. If you look at sport as a sport, then it will be far better. See, some amount of chit chat happens, and has been happening for a long time. That should happen also.The game needs a bit of masala (spice) like that. However, it should not reach a point where you feel it is shameful. So, somewhere down the line, I think that the ICC and the respective boards need to put their foot forward and say, 'this is not done.' 'You try hard on the field to win the match for your team, try your best, but after the match, those reactions, I don't think are the right ones. Both from our side and their side," Harbhajan told reporters at an event at the BPGC Golf Course here on Tuesday.Asked specifically about Rana's on-field clashes with Pakistan's players, Harbhajan quipped, "I don't think that should happen. I think it is not setting the right example for the generation coming up."While he wasn't critical of India's bowlers' inability to take New Zealand's eight remaining wickets on the final day of the first Test at Wellington, which ended in a draw on Monday, calling the pitch "really flat," Harbhajan, who took 417 wickets in 103 Tests (1998-2015), wasn't entirely convinced about India's decision to shake hands with their Kiwi counterparts even with 15 overs left to be bowled in the last session of the match, and felt that they could have continued bowling. "I thought the pitch was dry and very flat. It's okay. Pitches in Australia and New Zealand tend to be really flat, at times.“I think a lot has been talked about in this game. There were 15 overs left and they declared the game (a draw) before. Yes, you could have tried. You never know. Things move very fast in cricket. But somewhere down the line, you have to be honest with yourself, as a captain and management, whether it was the right decision on that pitch or in that scenario. I think that a lot of thought would have gone into that decision. But if I was part of the management, I would have liked to bowl another 15 overs and give it a try. And let's see. You never know,” Harbhajan said.Recalling how former Australia captain Michael Clarke, with his part-time left-arm spin, had bowled Australia to a win against India in the closing minutes of the controversial Sydney Test in January 2008, taking three for five in 1.5 overs, the former tweaker said, "After everyone else had bowled, Australia introduced Clarke just two overs before (the close of the Test). And nothing was happening. Suddenly he came and he took those two important wickets and they ended up winning that match. So, cricket is a very funny game. Anything can happen."Citing the fighting attitude of his former India spin-bowling partner and ex-India captain Anil Kumble, Harbhajan said, "I have always been a fan of Anil Bhai. And I still say that his attitude was that you have to fight till the last ball. Whether you are bowling or batting or in the field, you have to fight till the last ball. So 90 balls is a lot. I think we should have tried in those 90 balls (to get the remaining five Kiwi wickets). You never know. Maybe the result will come in your favour."Harbhajan defended off-spinner Washington Sundar, who took one for 65 in 35 overs as the Kiwis secured a draw in the first Test. "It's very easy for all of us to pinpoint an individual and say he could have done this or he could have done that. I will put myself in his position. He tried his best. He is young. He is learning. And of course, the more he plays, the more he will learn about these situations. Next time, if he is in such a situation, I am sure he will be able to perform better. So, let's not pinpoint an individual. You win with 11, you lose with 11 and you throw with 11. He must have tried. If it was me, I would have tried as well. So, give him some time. I am sure he will learn and he will get better," Harbhajan stressed.Critics have panned India's inability to close out Test wins in their last two games by taking wickets on the fifth and final day — it happened against Sri Lanka in Colombo in August, and then against New Zealand on the final day of the first Test at Wellington. Harbhajan, though, isn't perturbed and urged fans to "have some patience with the Indian team.""That will happen (closing out Test wins). This is the same team that won in England (India drew the Test series 2-2 last summer in England). Have some patience with the team. We have a trend here. If you don't get a result that we want from the Indian team, then we go after it. Give them a break. They need to 'breathe out' as well. They are on the road continuously. So, give them some break. I'm sure that they'll get the right results for Team India. "Would it have made a difference if Ravindra Jadeja and Mohammed Siraj had played? "Time will tell. You say, what would have happened if Kapil paaji had played? I can't say much about what would have happened. But if he would have played, we would have talked about it. I can't really predict what would have happened if he would have played. If I would have known, I would have called Gautam and asked him to play," Harbhajan retorted.Talking about the ongoing 'Sandpaper-gate' controversy rearing its head in Australian cricket again, Harbhajan felt that it "wasn't a new thing" and that it showed that the Australian team sometimes received far more respect than they deserved."I don't think this is a new thing. This is a very old thing. Pakistan and India have been talking about this for a long time. That this is a reverse swing.We are making such a big thing about this. Australia was doing it before. England was doing it. South Africa was doing it. Wherever there is reverse swing, there must be something with the ball. People are doing it. How much they do it naturally, or the way they have done it with sandpaper, that is a little bad.Naturally, if you go to make the ball reverse, it takes some time to get the ball going. But if you make the ball reverse in the 10th over, then it is understood that there can be nothing but teasing."Australia is not as simple as they used to be. Their players are not as simple as they used to be. I have said this from day one, they should not be given so much respect. They should be given a lot of respect. They have also played the game. They have also done all these things. Now they have been caught or things have come out, they are saying that they did not know. It is not possible that you are living in one house, you are living in another house, you do not know who is living there. Everybody was part of it. I believe. If it is in the team, then it is a collective thing."
Article Summary: Harbhajan Singh has joined the chorus of those voicing their concern at the deteriorating player behaviour during India-Pakistan clashes. India's off-spin great has urged the game's authorities to "step in" to check the trend of players from both countries getting carried away in Indo-Pak cricket matches.

Article Title: BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships: Amid personal loss, Priya Sheoran hopes to make her mark
Article Text:
(From left) Bhartpreet Singh, Rahul Sarnaliya, Sadhna Ravi, Priya

The past few months have tested Priya Sheoran in ways far beyond the athletics field.The Haryana discus thrower had been making frequent trips to hospital as her father Anup, a sub-inspector with Haryana Police and the man who inspired her to take up sports, had been unwell for several months. He passed away on Nov 10.Barely a fortnight later, Priya is set to step into the competition arena again, carrying both the grief of her loss and the hope of putting up a strong performance at the three-day inaugural BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships to be held at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar from Wednesday.“For the past four months, I had been going back and forth to the hospital with him. So, the preparation hasn’t been that good, but let’s hope for the best,” said Priya.The youngster, who has trained under celebrated discus thrower Seema Punia, won bronze at the U23 Asian Athletics Championships earlier this year, her first international medal.“It felt really good because it was my first international medal. This tournament is also being organised for the first time, so I’ll try to perform well here too and hopefully win a medal,” said the 22-year-old.Given what she has been through in recent months, Priya is trying not to burden herself with expectations.“I just want to put my best foot forward and give my best. I haven’t really thought about the result yet. I’ll go in with the mindset that I have to perform well,” she added.Priya will be among a 70-member Indian contingent looking to make an impression at the event.A little more than 200 athletes from six countries are expected to compete in the three-day event. With Thailand pulling out, athletes from Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Nepal and Sri Lanka will join hosts India in the competition.Among those attracting attention will also be 17-year-old sprinter Neil Samraj, who comes into the event on the back of a record-breaking season.Samraj broke the U18 national record in the 100m twice in a single day at the National Youth Athletics Championships in Ludhiana, eventually clocking 10.46s in the final. He lowered the mark further at the National Junior Athletics Championships in Chennai last month, running 10.45s. He also rewrote the U18 national record in the 200m in Chennai with a time of 21.03 seconds.Now, with an opportunity to test himself against athletes from the region, Samraj wants to see where he stands at the end of a long season.“Competing internationally will help me gain experience and prepare for many more international competitions where I will be up against athletes from different countries,” Samraj said in a social media post released by the Athletics Federation of India.“The plan is just to go hard because this is a very good opportunity to participate in a regional international competition. It will also help me understand where I stand and what kind of timings I can produce towards the end of the season.”For India’s young athletes, the championships provide another international opportunity at the end of a season that has witnessed several national records tumble. For Priya, however, simply returning to the throwing circle after a difficult few months will carry a significance of its own.
Article Summary: Priya Sheoran to compete at BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar. Haryana discus thrower will be carrying the grief of her father's death. Priya won bronze at the U23 Asian Athletics Championships earlier this year.

Gulf Giants continued their winning start to the ILT20 Season 5, registering a six-wicket victory over MI Emirates at the Dubai International Stadium on Tuesday after bowling them out for just 91.ILT20 debutant Shamar Joseph and David Wiese claimed three wickets each as MI Emirates were dismissed in 19.3 overs for their lowest total in the league. The 91 was also the joint-second lowest score recorded in Dubai in ILT20 history.Shamar returned figures of 3/9, while Wiese finished with 3/19. Alzarri Joseph, Azmatullah Omarzai and Haider Razzaq picked up a wicket each as Gulf Giants kept MI Emirates in check throughout the innings.The chase was far from straightforward initially, with Gulf Giants losing Rahmanullah Gurbaz (0) and Liam Livingstone (1) inside the first two overs. Omarzai (6) and Dhruv Parashar (15) also fell, leaving the Giants at 50/4.However, Ibrahim Zadran and Heinrich Klaasen steadied the innings with an unbeaten 43-run partnership to take Gulf Giants home in 13.5 overs.Zadran finished on 50 not out from 35 balls, hitting five fours and a six, while Klaasen contributed 16 off 16 deliveries, including a four and a six.Earlier, MI Emirates suffered an early setback when Muhammad Waseem (4) was bowled by Omarzai in the opening over.Shamar then struck twice in the fourth over, removing Kusal Perera (6) and Sanjay Krishnamurthi (0), before dismissing Sherfane Rutherford (1) in the final over of the powerplay.MI Emirates were reduced to 22/4, with Shamar having conceded no runs until his fourth wicket.Nicholas Pooran attempted to revive the innings with Kieron Pollard, but their 29-run stand was broken by Wiese in the 12th over. Pooran departed for 23 off 34 balls, while Pollard was dismissed for 13 by Haider Razzaq in the following over.Rashid Khan (7), Romario Shepherd (13) and Jordan Thompson (3) offered little resistance as MI Emirates continued to lose wickets. Wiese removed Thompson in the 18th over before the innings ended at 91 in 19.3 overs.Player of the Match, Gulf Giants' Shamar Joseph said, "I thought it was simple. I saw Omarzai bowling and the ball was seaming and swinging. It's my debut here, and I'm feeling amazing about what I did. Our chances are good. You meet new people, and a lot of them have played around the world, which helps me. Getting information on the conditions is important."MI Emirates skipper Kieron Pollard said, "We lost a couple of wickets in clusters. You practice for scenarios and conditions, so you don't use pitches as an excuse. I told the bowlers not to look for magic balls. I fielded at short leg numerous times just to try and put pressure on the opponents.There's no need to dissect it much, as it was tough for both sides' batters."(Nicholas Pooran 23, Kieron Pollard 13, Romario Shepherd 13, Shamar Joseph 3 for 9, David Wiese 3 for 19)(Ibrahim Zadran 50*, Heinrich Klaasen 16*, Dhruv Parashar 15, Jordan Thompson 2 for 27, Fazalhaq Farooqi 1 for 21)
Article Summary: ILT20 debutant Shamar Joseph and David Wiese claimed three wickets each as MI Emirates were dismissed in 19.3 overs for their lowest total in the league. Ibrahim Zadran and Heinrich Klaasen steadied the innings with an unbeaten 43-run partnership.

The Indian Street Premier League (ISPL) will move to Goa for its fourth season, with the tennis-ball T10 tournament scheduled to run from December 6, 2026, to January 3, 2027. Eight franchises will compete in 44 matches at the 1919 Sportz Cricket Stadium in Verna.Defending champions Chennai Singams will open the season against last year's runners-up Tiigers of Kolkata on December 6, setting up a rematch of the Season 3 final. The final is scheduled for January 3, 2027.Single-header matches will begin at 8pm, while double-header days will start at 5:30pm.The move to Goa comes as the league looks to expand its reach and strengthen its grassroots talent pathway. Across its first three editions, ISPL has provided a platform for aspiring cricketers from different parts of the country to showcase their abilities in the tennis-ball format.The Season 4 auction also reflected the league's growing commercial footprint, with the eight franchises collectively spending more than ₹10.40 crore.ISPL League Commissioner Suraj Samat said Goa's tourist season offered an opportunity to bring sport and tourism together while continuing to develop the league's talent pool.“Goa offers a fantastic setting for ISPL Season 4, with the schedule also coinciding with the state’s peak tourist season. This presents a natural opportunity for the league to flourish at the intersection of sport and tourism,” Samat said.The league has also revised its player selection process, removing simulation matches and introducing a data-driven system based on performances in local tournaments across the country. The top 500 performers will qualify for the auction pool through points accumulated in these competitions, alongside the top 50 contracted players.The revised process is intended to reduce human intervention and provide a performance-based route for grassroots players to enter the league.
Article Summary: ISPL Season 4 will begin on December 6, 2026 and will be played in Goa. All matches are played in the Indian Super League (ISL) The finals will be held on January 3, 2027. The final will take place at the Maracana in Mumbai.

Article Title: 102 matches, over five-thousand runs: Former India U19 World Cup winner quits first-class cricket at 32
Article Text:
Tamil Nadu's Baba Aparajith celebrates his century against Chhattisgarh during a Ranji Trophy cricket match at Nehru Stadium, in Guwahati. (PTI File Photo)

Former India Under-19 World Cup-winning all-rounder Baba Aparajith has retired from first-class cricket at the age of 32, ending a career in which he represented Tamil Nadu, Kerala and India A, besides being part of Chennai Super Kings and Rising Pune Supergiant in the IPL.Aparajith announced his retirement through an Instagram post on Wednesday, revealing that his last first-class match was played on January 24, 2026."I played my last first-class cricket match on January 24, 2026, officially bringing my first-class cricketing career to a close. Looking back, it has been an incredible journey filled with experiences, challenges, lessons, friendships and memories that I will cherish for a lifetime. It has been an absolute privilege to represent Tamil Nadu, India Under-19, India A, Kerala, Chennai Super Kings, Rising Pune Supergiant, TNPL franchises and my club teams, and to be part of the many teams and dressing rooms that have shaped my journey. Each experience has played a significant role in shaping me, both as a cricketer and as a person," he wrote on Instagram.Aparajith was part of India's Under-19 World Cup-winning team in 2012.He scored 171 runs and took five wickets during the tournament, finishing as India's fourth-highest run-scorer. He also won the Man-of-the-Match award in the quarter-final against Pakistan Under-19s and the semi-final against New Zealand Under-19s.The batting all-rounder made his Ranji Trophy debut for Tamil Nadu at the age of 17 before representing India Under-19s at the World Cup in Australia in 2012. He later broke into the India A setup in 2015 but could not establish himself consistently at that level.Aparajith was part of Chennai Super Kings for three consecutive seasons between 2013 and 2015 but never made his IPL debut for the franchise. He was also part of Rising Pune Supergiant in the league. However, he was largely viewed as an accumulator, with his overall strike rate of 108 across 63 T20 matches reflecting his batting approach.He played 102 first-class matches, most of them for Tamil Nadu, scoring 12 centuries and 27 half-centuries. He also contributed with his off-spin and had the opportunity to captain Tamil Nadu.Aparajith was part of three title-winning Tamil Nadu squads, winning the Vijay Hazare Trophy in 2017-18 and the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy in 2020-21 and 2021-22. He also represented Kerala during the final phase of his domestic career.Aparajith, whose twin brother Baba Indrajith is also a cricketer, thanked the cricketing bodies, his family, coaches, teammates and support staff for their backing throughout his career."My sincere gratitude to the BCCI, TNCA and KCA for the opportunities and support throughout my career. A special mention to my wife, my parents, my brother, my extended family, and all my friends and well-wishers for their unconditional support, sacrifices and belief in me throughout this journey. I’m grateful to my coaches, support staff and teammates who have been an integral part of this journey. My connection with the game will remain as strong as ever. I look forward to carrying forward the knowledge, experiences and lessons gathered over the years, continuing to learn, contribute and hopefully make a meaningful impact on the game in the years ahead," he added.
Article Summary: Baba Aparajith retires from first-class cricket at the age of 32. The all- rounder represented Tamil Nadu, Kerala and India A. He was also part of Chennai Super Kings and Rising Pune Supergiant in IPL. He won the Man-of-the-Match award at the 2012 Under-19 World Cup.

Article Title: 'Deny until you die': Now, Ben Stokes takes aim at Sandpapergate as row spills over
Article Text:
Usman Khawaja, Ben Stokes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former England captain Ben Stokes has urged Australian players involved in the Sandpapergate controversy to stop their public exchanges, saying the renewed debate is affecting people beyond those who took part in the incident.The ball-tampering scandal, which took place during Australia's 2018 Test series in South Africa, has returned to the spotlight 8 1/2 years later following the publication of former opener Usman Khawaja 's autobiography. The latest revelations have once again divided Australian cricket, with players offering conflicting accounts of what happened.“For the sake of players, the staff, the management who were involved in this whole situation, for the sake of their families, for the sake of their friends, the best thing for it to do now would be for it just to just to stop,” Stokes said on his “That's Not Cricket” podcast on Wednesday. “It’s affecting people who do not deserve to be affected by this.”Stokes' comments carry significance given the rivalry between England and Australia, two of cricket's oldest opponents. The teams will mark 150 years since their first Test match next March.Stokes played a key role for England over a 15-year international career, which included World Cup titles in the 50-over and T20 formats, performances that became part of Ashes history and his captaincy during the Bazball era.He has also been involved in incidents away from cricket that attracted media attention. Stokes was found not guilty of affray (assault) in 2018 following a late-night street fight in Bristol, southwest England, after England's win over the West Indies. He was also dropped for a match against New Zealand following a nightclub incident in June. He returned to the team before announcing his sudden retirement.Speaking about the impact of Sandpapergate, Stokes said the controversy had affected more than just the players involved.“Because I’ve been through something like this when you are so heavily in the media for something, I’ve seen what it’s done to people who don’t deserve to be put through stress, put through anxiety,” Stokes said. “Whoever was in charge of Cricket Australia at the time have a lot to answer for this.”The latest debate has seen players and members of the support staff involved in the 2018 South Africa Test series offer different versions of events. Three Australian players were handed bans after the ball-tampering incident, but Khawaja has written in his autobiography that the entire team knew about the plan and should have accepted collective responsibility.Current Australia captain Pat Cummins is among those who have denied knowing about the plan.“It’s got so deep into it ... that it’s almost just like ‘deny until you die’ one way or the other,” Stokes said. “I’ve been in the dressing room for long enough to form my own very well educated guess on what I think has happened, but I don’t think in the close future we're going to hear what truly happened because it’s just so deep.”Meanwhile, Cricket Australia has backed Cummins to continue as Test captain ahead of next month's series against New Zealand. The decision has ended speculation over his position amid the conflicting accounts of what he knew during the 2018 South Africa series.Cricket Australia chairman David Boon and chief executive Todd Greenberg issued a statement on Cummins' captaincy after the board announced that players from the 2018 series would be invited to take part in an independent forum and share their accounts of the incident.Cummins took over as Test captain from Tim Paine in late 2021. Paine had been appointed to the role in the aftermath of Sandpapergate.Steve Smith and David Warner , who were Australia's captain and vice-captain during the 2018 series, were banned for 12 months by Cricket Australia following the public reaction to the scandal. Cameron Bancroft, who was caught on television footage with sandpaper, received a nine-month suspension.Cummins' account of the incident has been challenged by Bancroft and Warner.
Article Summary: Former England captain Ben Stokes urges Australian players involved in Sandpapergate controversy to stop their public exchanges. Stokes says the renewed debate is affecting people beyond those who took part in the incident. The ball-tampering scandal took place during Australia's 2018 Test series in South Africa. The latest revelations have once again divided Australian cricket.

CHRISTCHURCH: India's only net session before the second Test against New Zealand was turning out to be quite a dampener because of relentless rain. The team reached Hagley Oval amidst steady drizzle, and the first batch, KL Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal and Dhruv Jurel, was forced to hit the AstroTurf in the indoor nets. There wasn't much to do, and the side-armers allowed the batters to get a feel for the ball before the skies above cleared to make way for some sunshine. The ground staff turned the training square around in miraculous time, and the players were able to get a proper hit before the final game of the tour.Away from the group, bowlers Jasprit Bumrah, Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna were in the main ground doing release work. The bowling pack was the centre of attention as it was the only department India are likely to tinker with for the must-win clash. Bowling coach Morne Morkel didn't offer any hints, but there were enough cues from the nets to convey the strong possibility of Gurnoor Brar making his Test debut.He operated with a lot of heat against captain Shubman Gill, and while it's unusual for a fast bowler to run in with that intensity on the eve of the match, Brar was probably showing his rhythm.A short burst later, he was asked to take it easy, and a short conversation followed between captain Shubman Gill and head coach Gautam Gambhir. Minutes later, Gambhir had a few words for the young bowler, who rushed to pad up for a decent hit.Interestingly, he was the only bowler from the entire squad to get some batting done and was closely watched by Gambhir. With the pitch expected to ease out for batting as the game progresses, the think tank is strongly pondering adding a few more yards to their attack. When asked about Brar's readiness, Morkel asserted that he is good to go and will be ideal for these conditions."There's a lot of excitement about him since he joined the Indian team because of his pace and bounce. He's a guy that will be well-suited to the conditions here. So, yeah, we'll see how it goes. He is knocking on the door, he is doing the right things. He has the bounce, pace and skill, and these conditions would suit him," said Morkel without revealing much about the Playing XI."He needs to just make sure he's ready when he gets the opportunity. I think a lot of times, we think we want that opportunity. We want to be close, and as a bowler, you can get distracted. When he gets his opportunity, which is... You know, we never know. My job is to make sure he's 100% ready when he gets that opportunity," he further added.India persisted with Prasidh Krishna as their only tall fast bowler for the series opener, but the returns were far from encouraging in the first innings. He failed to pose any major threat on the "lifeless pitch", and even though the reading improved in the second innings, it doesn't reveal the entire story. Prasidh was economical, bowled 10 maidens, but the spell came at a time when the opposition pair of Darryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips was happy to eat time and never looked like scoring.With both Kamboj and Akash offering value with the bat, and the team's obsession with depth, the only change likely at this stage is Brar coming in for Prasidh. There could be a late twist in the selection tale depending on what they make of the pitch on the morning of the game, but the cues on match eve didn't point in that direction.In Brar, Gill would get an attacking bowler in good form, with the ability to operate in the higher 140s. Pace has been captain Gill's obsession, and he now has the opportunity to unleash the bowler he has been grooming for the role which the team badly wants him to perform.
Article Summary: India's only net session before the second Test against New Zealand was turning out to be quite a dampener because of relentless rain. Bowling coach Morne Morkel didn't offer any hints, but there were enough cues from the nets to convey the strong possibility of Gurnoor Brar making his Test debut. India persisted with Prasidh Krishna as their only tall fast bowler for the series opener.

India wicketkeeper-batter Rishabh Pant took part in a local cricket match in Christchurch on Wednesday, using the opportunity to to keep his eye sharp ahead of the second New Zealand Test starting Friday.Pant, 29, is one of the leading six-hitters in Test cricket history. The match ended in a draw.Pant's appearance in a local Last Man Stands match came after he was spotted in central Christchurch.One team, Open House Swingers, were down a player and asked Pant if he would fill in, with the Indian star wasting no time picking up the bat to give them a boost.He turned out for the Open House Swingers against The Chosen Ones at Hagley Park. NEW DELHI: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's stunning double-century against the UAE has taken the cricket world by surprise. The 15-year-old smashed 204 off just 53 balls for India A in the Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026, leaving fans and former cricketers amazed.Even Iceland Cricket joined the conversation with a hilarious post on social media, bringing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang into the discussion. The cricket board joked that Sooryavanshi's bat was powered by artificial intelligence (AI) chips."It's no coincidence that on Tuesday Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia CEO and on Wednesday, the AI chips in Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's bat came back," Iceland Cricket posted on X.Sooryavanshi's innings included 28 sixes and helped him break several records in List A cricket. He now holds the record for the fastest double-century in the format, reaching the 200-run mark in just 52 balls.The young left-hander's knock was special not just because of the number of runs he scored but also because of the speed at which he reached the milestones.Fastest double-centuries in List A cricket: Sooryavanshi reached 200 in 52 balls against the UAE in 2026.Chad Bowes is second on the list with a 103-ball double-century for Canterbury against Otago in 2024. N Jagadeesan and Harry Brook have also scored double-centuries in 114 balls.Most sixes in a professional cricket innings: Sooryavanshi's 28 sixes are now the most in all professional cricket. Tanmay Agarwal is second with 26 sixes for Hyderabad against Arunachal Pradesh in the Ranji Trophy in 2024.Most sixes in a List A innings: Sooryavanshi leads the list with 28 sixes. D'Arcy Short had hit 23 for Western Australia against Queensland in 2018, while Bevon Jacobs struck 21 for Auckland against Otago in 2026.His 28-ball century and his 150-run milestone were also the fastest in List A cricket. The 150-run mark broke a record that Sooryavanshi himself had previously held. His strike rate of 384.90 is also the highest recorded for a List A century.After his record-breaking performance, Sooryavanshi revealed that a half-hour conversation with former India all-rounder Yuvraj Singh helped him overcome a difficult period and regain his confidence.The youngster said he spoke to four people before the match against the UAE, including his father, childhood coach Manish Ojha, friend Pratham Jachak and Yuvraj."I spoke to only four people (before going into the match). Of course, I spoke to my father. Then my childhood coach, Manish Ojha and my friend, who was with me from the Under-19s - his name is Pratham Jachak. The fourth one is Yuvraj (Singh) sir. I spoke to him for almost half-an-hour," Sooryavanshi said in a video posted on bcci.tv.on Wednesday.Yuvraj has also guided young Indian batters such as Abhishek Sharma and Shubman Gill. Sooryavanshi said he openly discussed the problems he was facing with his batting, and the former India all-rounder gave him technical advice."He explained a lot of things about my batting. He mainly told me, 'If you bat for 20 balls, the team's score will be different'. He told me a lot of technical things. All of that helped me a lot."

Article Title: Batter leaves stumps unattended, gets bowled off a 'free ball': What is BBL's little-known timed-out rule that saw Deandra Dottin walk back without batting?
Article Text:
Photo/screengrab

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Melbourne Renegades survived a scare to keep their Women's Big Bash League (WBBL) campaign alive, beating Brisbane Heat by three wickets in a last-ball finish after Deandra Dottin became the first player to be dismissed under the competition's timed-out rule.Chasing Heat's total of 137/8, the Renegades were in control at 3-97 before Sarah Glenn dismissed Georgia Wareham. Dottin then walked in but was penalised for taking more than the permitted time to get ready to face the ball.Under BBL rules, a batter must be ready to face the next delivery within 75 seconds of the previous dismissal. However, the timed-out rule in the competition has an additional provision: the incoming batter must stand to the side while the opposition bowler gets a free delivery at the stumps.Glenn made the most of the opportunity, hitting the stumps with her free delivery to dismiss Dottin without her facing a ball. The Renegades had slipped from 3-97 to 5-97 in the space of two deliveries.“This is great drama. Dottin’s out! She was late to the crease and she’s out without facing a ball,” Fox Cricket commentator Corbin Middlemas said. “What a blunder.”The rule was introduced in the 2021-22 season but had not been enforced before, despite several instances of players taking longer than the permitted time.Brisbane Heat batter Grace Harris had little sympathy for Dottin, saying professional players should know better.“No, I haven’t seen it in the game. I know there’s been a rule. If you want some directness. This is professional cricket, not park cricket,” Harris said, as quoted by Fox Cricket.Despite the setback, the Renegades completed the chase, winning by three wickets off the final ball. Annie Wikman, who remained unbeaten on eight off five balls, guided them home after they needed nine runs from the final over. She had also taken three catches during the Heat innings.Earlier, Sophie Molineux took 4-20, dismissing Charli Knott (15) and Harris (0) bowled before claiming two more wickets in three deliveries. The performance also made her the Renegades' all-time leading wicket-taker.The Heat had recovered from 4-59 to reach 4-90 before Molineux struck again to slow their progress.The win lifted the Renegades to fourth place in the standings, but they must beat Melbourne Stars on Saturday to secure a place in the finals.
Article Summary: Melbourne Renegades beat Brisbane Heat by three wickets in WBBL. Deandra Dottin becomes first player to be dismissed under timed-out rule. Under BBL rules, a batter must be ready to face the next delivery within 75 seconds of the previous dismissal.

Article Title: Best ever! From 14 medals to 114: How India achieved more with fewer athletes at the Asian Para Games
Article Text:
Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

From 14 medals to 114: India's remarkable rise

India's Asian Para Games record

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Smaller contingent, bigger return

Hangzhou vs Aichi-Nagoya

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Athletics powers India's medal surge

India's leading medal-winning sports in Asian Para Games 2026

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Multiple medallists underline India's depth

Paralympic progress provides the wider context

Fourth place sets a new benchmark

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, India’s remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece.India’s campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally.But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event.The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings.More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years — from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations.India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally.At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals — one gold, four silver and nine bronze — to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings.The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth.Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth.Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth.The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth.The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough.The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals.India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals.The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged.On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports.Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success; it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport.Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish.Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total.Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze.Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals.Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals.That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions.India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports.Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul.Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds.Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally.The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad.India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport.At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals — five gold, eight silver and six bronze — lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th.The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings.India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving.China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold.India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze.The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games.The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines.For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport — one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi- Nagoya. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place. It is the best finish in the country's history at the event.

Article Text:

Third Paralympics, one big dream: Gold at LA 2028

IAS officer by day, shuttler by night

NEW DELHI: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. Having beaten Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan in their group match just days earlier, the Indian shuttler had hoped to reach the final and fight for gold.Suhas lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23-21, 8-21, 15-21. He had chances to take the opening game but failed to convert them. After bouncing back to win the second game 21-8, he lost focus at a crucial stage of the decider.“Definitely not satisfied with bronze. I think if I had played up to my full potential, I would have definitely done better. In fact, I defeated Fredy of Indonesia in the group match in Nagoya only a few days ago,” Suhas told TimesofIndia.com from Aichi-Nagoya in Japan.“In the semifinal match, the first set was very close. I lost 23-21 and I had game point, set point, but I couldn't convert that. In the second set, I won very easily. In the third set, I think after 10-all, I sort of lost focus for two to three rallies. That is where he took the game. So, it was not my best day, I would assume. I would always love to win a gold medal. So, yes, I am a little sad from that angle,” he said.The defeat also reminded him of how important it is to perform under pressure at major tournaments.“It is the most important factor to win medals at major games because you might be training well, you might actually have the fitness and the skills. But if you don't recreate that during the major games, then probably it is of not much use in terms of professional success,” Suhas said.Suhas, an IAS officer, said he had never imagined representing India in international badminton a decade ago.In November 2016, he made his debut at the Asian Championships in Beijing and won gold. Since then, he has won several medals at major international events. These include bronze at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, silver at the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics, another silver at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, gold at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games and bronze in Nagoya.The 43-year-old has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024, winning silver on both occasions.With the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics approaching, the big question is whether he can go one step further and win gold.The desire is there, but Suhas is not looking too far ahead. He wants to take things one step at a time.“If you had asked me 10 years ago, I didn't even know that I would play for India. But whenever I look at the medals and the love I have got from fans and sportspersons around the world, the journey has been quite satisfying. I have had the honour of wearing the Indian jersey and winning medals for my country,” he said.“I am grateful for what God has given me. I never imagined that I would become an IAS officer one day, an Arjuna awardee or a badminton player winning medals for India. I never imagined all this. But thanks to the Almighty for all these,” Suhas, who is also an Arjuna Award recipient, said.“So if God and destiny have been kind to me, I hope they will take me to a place that I deserve. I hope I can do the best that I can in whatever I choose to,” he added.For most people, the end of a hectic working day is a time to relax, spend time with family, play with their children or watch a movie.For Suhas, it is often time to pick up his badminton racket and head to the court. His day includes early-morning gym sessions, office work, inspections, meetings, video conferences and checking files. Despite his demanding responsibilities as an IAS officer, he makes time for badminton and follows a strict fitness routine to compete at the highest level.Balancing the two careers is not easy, but his love for the sport keeps him going.“If you choose what you love, then the journey becomes painless. You enjoy that journey. That's what I do,” Suhas said.Explaining how he manages his work and training, he said: “It is challenging. My training generally starts in the night and it always involves sacrifices. Probably others would be spending time with their family members or having leisure time. My leisure time is to play badminton. In badminton, you need an extremely high level of fitness. It's challenging, hectic but at the same time I love it.”“I don't remember eating sweets in the last many months. I can't recall when I had my last sweet. So, I almost don't eat sweets or fried food and am also quite conscious about the nutrition that I take,” he said.Suhas grew up watching Malaysian badminton great Lee Chong Wei and was inspired by his movement on the court.“Yes, I have always been inspired by so many top players in the able-bodied category. Growing up, I watched the matches of Lee Chong Wei and how he used to move around the court,” he said.“Even in India, the top shuttlers perform extremely well, whether it is Lakshya Sen, HS Prannoy or Kidambi Srikanth. I know them personally and have always admired how well they are able to compete at the top,” Suhas signed off.
Article Summary: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. The Indian shuttler lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23- 21, 8-21, 15-21. Suhas has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024.

NEW DELHI: India signed off from the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games with their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals as the week-long continental competition concluded with a closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday.Double gold medallists Nishad Kumar and Mona Agarwal led the Indian contingent as flag-bearers at the ceremony, marking the end of a landmark campaign in which the country's para-athletes delivered historic victories, world-record performances and podium sweeps across disciplines.India finished fourth in the overall standings with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, surpassing its previous best of 108 medals at the 2022 Hangzhou Games.Held in Japan for the first time, the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games brought together around 4,000 athletes and staff from 45 countries and regions. The competition featured 18 sports, with more than 20 world records reportedly set during the seven-day event.China topped the medal table with 435 medals, including 207 gold, while hosts Japan finished second with 186 medals — 64 gold, 60 silver and 62 bronze.Uzbekistan emerged as the third-ranked nation, collecting 145 medals, including 45 gold.India's fourth-place finish was particularly significant given the size of its contingent. A total of 168 para-athletes represented the country at Aichi-Nagoya, compared with 309 at the previous edition in Hangzhou.President Droupadi Murmu congratulated the Indian contingent on its record performance, saying the achievement reflected the athletes' hard work, perseverance and self-belief.In a post on X, Murmu said the unprecedented medal haul would inspire young people to dream big, work with dedication and remain positive in the face of challenges. She also extended her congratulations to the entire Indian contingent.Para athletics was India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. Para badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze.India also won 11 medals in para swimming, seven in para table tennis, six in para archery and five in para shooting. The contingent added two medals each in para judo and para powerlifting.The closing ceremony brought together athletes, officials and dignitaries to mark the conclusion of the Games. Asian Paralympic Committee president Majid Rashed declared the event closed, highlighting the growing strength of para sport across Asia and its role in building a more inclusive society.Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also praised the athletes' determination, teamwork and sportsmanship, describing their performances as a reminder of the “profound beauty” of para sports.The Asian Para Games began in Guangzhou, China, in 2010, evolving from the Far East and South Pacific Games Federation for the Disabled. The Aichi-Nagoya edition was the fifth staging of the event, with Doha, Qatar, scheduled to host the sixth in 2030.For India, the closing ceremony marked the end of a historic campaign — one that raised the country's medal benchmark and showcased the depth and growing strength of its para-sport movement.

Article Title: Navdeep Singh credits SAI JLN Stadium support as India deliver record Asian Para Games medal haul
